approach: Add one read-only engine beside its project-spec siblings and wire it into the per-project entry point; introduce no new spec location, no new gate, no lifecycle write.
Settle the extraction rule from a throwaway spike over two live corpora before drafting, so the scope of what counts as a reference is evidence rather than a guess.
Earn the escape hatch: ship it only for the false-positive class the spike actually produced twice, and keep it inline beside the prose it excuses rather than in a registry that drifts.
Fix the survivors the first run finds in this repo's own corpus in the same change; allow-list none of them.

title: Project-spec engine nodes each improvise their own Use Cases shape for a single-entry-point deterministic checker
why: Raised as an architect observation by the cold spec-judge. A deterministic checker has one invoking actor and a set of state conditions, which does not fit a use-case table keyed on actor and goal. One sibling omits the actor column entirely; this node first filled it inaccurately and then collapsed to one use case with extensions. Neither is wrong, but the corpus has no settled shape for the class, so each node negotiates it again. Whether these nodes want a lighter declared shape is a corpus-wide question, not this CR's - it would touch several frozen suites.

Within the auto-spec leash: purely additive, one read-only engine in an established family, no narrowing anywhere. Five cold judge rounds, four of which found a real defect, every one the same shape - a rule reaching further or less far than its stated reason, leaving somewhere a genuinely broken reference could hide silently. Round 1 stopped at preflight: three resolved-actor bars never loaded, and loading them found an audit mode that differed from the guard by exit code alone, a suite with no graph behind it, and a doubled-backtick exclusion that was a regex accident rather than a rule. Round 3 found a stray backtick swallowing the rest of its line. Round 4 found the escape hatch firing on a line that merely quoted it - which is how the node documents it - so the most-guarded piece of the design was self-triggering. Each was fixed at the rule and swept for its other instances rather than patched at the instance named. Two further defects came from my own mutation sweeps that no judge caught: the code-span run-length rule was load-bearing but untested, and a mistyped spec dir failed unhandled. Round 5 returned ALIGNED true on all three lenses after attacking the live extraction path with its own constructed inputs. Thirteen mutations each fail exactly the tests they should. The guard's first run caught what it was built for: 14 broken anchors across two repos, every one an off-by-one, each corrected against the tree rather than allow-listed.

title: A link target containing a literal close-paren truncates at the first one
why: Raised by the cold spec-judge at round 5 and confirmed. The inline-link pattern stops the target at the first close-paren, so a link whose filename carries balanced parens extracts a truncated path. The failure direction is over-reporting only - a valid link reported as broken, never a broken one passing - which is the opposite class from the one this engine guards, and no filename in either live corpus carries parens today. Fixing it means either matching balanced parens or accepting only the angle-bracket-wrapped form for such targets.

title: A four-space indented code block is not excluded from reference extraction the way a fence is
why: Raised by the cold spec-judge at round 5. Indented code blocks are CommonMark's other code-block form and carry samples just as fences do, but only fences are excluded. The failure direction is over-reporting only, and this corpus's style uses fences exclusively, so nothing fires today. It becomes real the moment a spec adopts indented blocks.
